events.title: Lex Ovinia: censors choose the Senate
events.summary: A tribunician law of Ovinius transferred the choice of senators from the consuls to the censors, who were to enrol 'the best men of every rank', in practice ex-magistrates; the Senate thus became a body of former office-holders with life membership.
events.detail: Festus is the only source and does not date the law; most scholars place it between 339 and 312, often just before the censorship of Appius Claudius (312), whose controversial enrolment of freedmen's sons may have been the first under the new rules. Before Ovinius, consuls or consular tribunes had chosen their advisers each year, and senators could be dropped (praeteriti). Afterwards the Senate gained continuity and independent authority, while the censors' lectio senatus, with its notae marking expelled members, became a powerful moral instrument (as in the expulsion of P. Cornelius Rufinus in 275).
scholarship: Cornell, 'The lex Ovinia and the emancipation of the Senate', in Bruun (ed.), The Roman Middle Republic (2000)
events.debate: Date (c. 339-312) and the meaning of 'ex omni ordine optimum quemque curiatim' are disputed.

events.title: Teanum Apulum and Canusium submit
events.summary: The Teates of Apulia obtained a treaty, Canusium gave hostages after its land was ravaged, and in 317 Forentum was taken; Rome now held a ring of allies around Samnium from Apulia, while in the same year prefects were first sent to Capua.
events.detail: Canusium was a rich Daunian city whose tombs, full of painted vases and gold, show a Hellenised native aristocracy. It remained loyal to Rome and sheltered the survivors of Cannae in 216.

events.title: Agathocles seizes power in Syracuse
events.summary: Agathocles, son of a potter from Thermae, twice exiled, returned with the backing of the Carthaginian general Hamilcar, led his troops in a massacre of about 4,000 members of the oligarchic Six Hundred and their supporters, drove 6,000 into exile, and was elected general with full powers.
events.detail: He promised to cancel debts and redistribute land, and ruled as tyrant and from 304 as king until 289. Timaeus, whom he exiled, wrote a bitterly hostile history; Duris of Samos and Callias were more favourable. Polybius, criticising Timaeus, conceded that Agathocles must have had extraordinary abilities. For Rome he matters as the precursor of Pyrrhus: a Greek warlord whose wars weakened Carthage, whose Campanian mercenaries became the Mamertines, and whose death opened the Sicilian vacuum that led to 264.

events.title: Q. Aemilius Barbula storms Nerulum
events.summary: The consul Q. Aemilius Barbula took the Lucanian town of Nerulum by storm, a sign that Rome's war against Samnium already reached into Lucania.
events.detail: Nerulum lay on the later Via Popilia route through the Lucanian highlands.

events.title: Fall of Saticula
events.summary: After a long siege begun in 316 by the dictator L. Aemilius, Saticula, a Samnite town on the edge of the Campanian plain, fell to the dictator Q. Fabius in 315, while the Samnites took Plistica in retaliation.
events.detail: A Latin colony was planted at Saticula in 313.

events.title: Recapture of Sora
events.summary: Sora, which had killed its Roman colonists and gone over to the Samnites, was retaken in 314 when a deserter led ten soldiers up to the citadel at night; 225 ringleaders were taken to Rome, scourged and beheaded in the Forum.
events.detail: Sora controlled the upper Liris valley, the route between Latium and Samnium; it was finally secured with a Latin colony in 303.

events.title: Acrotatus of Sparta at Acragas
events.summary: Acragas, Gela and Messana, allied against Agathocles, called in Acrotatus son of the Spartan king Cleomenes II as general; he proved luxurious and murderous, killing the exile leader Sosistratus at a banquet, and was stoned and driven out, after which Carthage brokered a peace that left Agathocles master of eastern Sicily.
events.detail: Acrotatus belongs to the line of Spartan royals hired by western Greeks, from Archidamus (338) to Cleonymus (303).

events.title: Capture of Nola
events.summary: Nola, the Oscan-Greek city east of Vesuvius that had sent its garrison to Palaepolis in 327, was taken in 313, by the dictator C. Poetelius according to most of Livy's sources; Atina and Calatia were taken in the same campaign.
events.detail: Nola became a loyal ally; it was the base from which Marcellus checked Hannibal in 216-214. Its coinage was Greek-style with the legend NOLAION.

events.title: The cult of the Ara Maxima made public
events.summary: The censor Appius Claudius persuaded the Potitii, hereditary priests of Hercules at the Ara Maxima with the Pinarii, to teach the rites to public slaves; within a year all twelve families of the Potitii, thirty adult men, were dead, and Appius later went blind, which pious tradition read as punishment.
events.detail: The change made the cult of Hercules, closely tied to the cattle market of the Forum Boarium and to tithes from traders, a state cult supervised by the urban praetor. Modern scholars see Appius bringing a lucrative gentilicial cult under public control. The Ara Maxima lay near the church of Santa Maria in Cosmedin.

events.title: The flute-players' strike
events.summary: Forbidden by the censors to hold their customary feast in the temple of Jupiter, the guild of flute-players, indispensable at every sacrifice, left for Tibur; the Tiburtines got them drunk at a banquet and carted them back to Rome asleep, and their feasting rights were restored, with three days of masked revelry each June.
events.detail: The Quinquatrus minusculae of 13-15 June preserved the episode. It shows a professional collegium using withdrawal, the plebeian tactic of secession, to defend its privileges, and the practical dependence of public ritual on specialists.

events.title: C. Junius Bubulcus takes Cluviae and Bovianum
events.summary: The consul C. Junius Bubulcus retook Cluviae, where the Samnites had tortured a Roman garrison to death, and sacked Bovianum, the chief town of the Pentri; escaping an ambush in a mountain pass, he vowed a temple to Salus.
events.detail: Bovianum fell again in 305 and 298, showing that Roman captures of Samnite towns were raids rather than permanent conquests until the 290s.

events.title: Treaties with Camerinum and Ocriculum
events.summary: Scouting beyond the Ciminian forest in 310, Fabius' brother reached the Umbrian Camertes, who offered alliance and received a treaty on equal terms; in 308 Ocriculum, on the Tiber, also obtained a treaty.
events.detail: Cicero cites the foedus with Camerinum as a model of an equal treaty, and in 205 the Camertes sent a cohort to Scipio as allies of equal right. The treaties split Umbria and gave Rome a corridor to the Adriatic behind Etruria.

events.title: First recorded Roman naval landing
events.summary: P. Cornelius, put in charge of the coast by the Senate, landed a naval force at Pompeii and ravaged the territory of Nuceria Alfaterna; on the way back, laden with booty, the raiders were attacked by country people and lost some men.
events.detail: This is the first recorded operation by the fleet whose officers, the duoviri navales, had been created in 311. Nuceria surrendered in 308.

events.title: The first Roman silver: the Mars/horse-head didrachm
events.summary: Rome's first silver coin, a didrachm of Greek weight (c. 7.3 g) showing a bearded helmeted Mars and a horse's head with the legend ROMANO, was struck in Campania, most likely at Neapolis; Burnett dates it c. 310-300, perhaps to pay for the Via Appia, while Crawford placed it c. 280-276.
events.detail: The issue is RRC 13/1 and was accompanied by a bronze litra. It belongs to the 'Romano-Campanian' series, of which the later Hercules/wolf-and-twins didrachm (traditionally associated with Pliny's date of 269) and the quadrigati followed. These coins were made for use in the Greek monetary world of southern Italy rather than in Rome itself, where bronze by weight and, from c. 280, cast aes grave remained the money. The debate over dates depends on hoard evidence from southern Italy and on links between Roman and Neapolitan dies.
scholarship: Burnett, 'The coinages of Rome and Magna Graecia', SNR 56 (1977)
Burnett, Coinage in the Roman World (1987)
events.debate: Date: c. 310-300 (Burnett) or c. 280-276 (Crawford); place of minting (Neapolis or Rome).

events.title: The eclipse of Agathocles' crossing
events.summary: As Agathocles' fleet slipped out of blockaded Syracuse for Africa, a total solar eclipse turned day into night and stars appeared everywhere; Agathocles told his frightened men it portended disaster for the enemy.
events.detail: Astronomers identify it with the eclipse of 15 August 310 BC, one of the fixed points of Hellenistic chronology. It confirms Diodorus' dating of the African expedition, and illustrates the use of eclipses to date ancient events, as with the eclipse 'around the 350th year' in Ennius.

events.title: Hamilcar's night assault on Syracuse
events.summary: While Agathocles campaigned in Africa, the Carthaginian general Hamilcar attempted a night assault on Syracuse by the Euryalus; the column fell into confusion, Hamilcar was captured, tortured and killed, and his head was sent to Agathocles, who displayed it before the Carthaginian camp.
events.detail: The defeat of the Punic siege by Agathocles' brother Antander and the citizen defenders showed the success of Agathocles' gamble in carrying the war to Africa.

battle.significance: Relieved Syracuse while Agathocles was in Africa.

events.title: Papirius Cursor and the gilded shields
events.summary: The dictator L. Papirius Cursor defeated a Samnite army arrayed in two divisions, one with gilded shields and multicoloured tunics, the other with silvered shields and white; the gilded shields decorated the bankers' shops in the Forum, and the Campanians dressed their gladiators in the captured Samnite armour, origin of the 'Samnite' gladiator.
events.detail: Livy's battle has the hallmarks of later elaboration, but Papirius' triumph of 309 is in the Fasti and the gilded shields displayed in the Forum were real objects known to later Romans. The story is the earliest evidence connecting gladiatorial types with defeated enemies.

sides.strength: two divisions, gilded and silvered shields

battle.significance: Restored Roman fortunes in Samnium after 310.

events.debate: Site unknown; details suspected to be annalistic decoration.

events.title: Agathocles murders Ophellas
events.summary: Ophellas, Ptolemy's governor of Cyrene, marched a great army with Athenian colonists and their families across the Syrtis to join Agathocles, who had promised him Africa; on arrival Agathocles killed him and took over his troops.
events.detail: Diodorus speaks of over 10,000 soldiers and as many non-combatants who suffered terribly in the two-month desert march. Ophellas had married an Athenian of the Philaid family, which drew settlers from Athens. Ptolemy recovered Cyrene soon after.

events.title: Bomilcar's attempted tyranny at Carthage
events.summary: In the crisis of Agathocles' invasion the Carthaginian general Bomilcar tried to make himself tyrant, leading troops into the city; the citizens fought from the rooftops, his men surrendered under an amnesty, and Bomilcar was crucified in the agora.
events.detail: Aristotle had praised Carthage for never suffering a tyranny; Bomilcar's attempt was the nearest it came. The episode shows Carthaginian suspicion of successful generals, a recurring theme that later shaped Hannibal's career.

events.title: Battle of Mevania
events.summary: When the Umbrians boasted they would march on Rome, Q. Fabius Rullianus hurried from Samnium to Mevania and attacked them before they could deploy; most of the Umbrian peoples surrendered.
events.detail: With the forty-year truce granted to Tarquinii and the treaty with Ocriculum, the victory closed the Etruscan-Umbrian war of 311-308.

battle.significance: Ended Umbrian resistance for a decade.

events.title: Censors build roads through the countryside
events.summary: The censors C. Junius Bubulcus and M. Valerius Maximus let contracts at public expense for roads through the fields, and Junius contracted the temple of Salus he had vowed; the Via Valeria toward Tibur and the Apennines is often attributed to Valerius.
events.detail: Five years after the Via Appia, the censors' road programme marks the start of state road-building as a regular instrument of control over newly won territory.
events.locName: Roads east of Rome toward Tibur
events.debate: Attribution of the Via Valeria to the censor of 307 is a modern inference.

events.title: Agathocles abandons his army in Africa
events.summary: After his son Archagathus' defeats in the interior, Agathocles fled secretly back to Sicily; the abandoned army killed his sons Archagathus and Heraclides and made terms with Carthage, and Agathocles massacred the soldiers' relatives in Syracuse.
events.detail: The expedition (310-307) had shown that Carthage's African heartland was vulnerable, a lesson Regulus (256) and Scipio (204) followed. In 306 a peace restored the status quo in Sicily, with Carthage paying Agathocles silver and grain.

events.title: Treaties with the Marsi, Paeligni, Marrucini, Frentani and Vestini
events.summary: After the annihilation of the Aequi, the Marrucini, Marsi, Paeligni and Frentani sent envoys seeking peace and friendship and received treaties; the Vestini followed in 302.
events.detail: These peoples of the central Apennines became Rome's most valued allies, supplying contingents for two centuries, and led the revolt of the Social War in 91, when their federal capital at Corfinium was renamed Italia.

events.title: Agathocles calls himself king
events.summary: Following Antigonus, Demetrius, Ptolemy, Seleucus and Cassander, who had assumed the royal title in 306-305, Agathocles began to style himself king (basileus), though he did not wear a diadem; his coins now read 'of King Agathocles'.
events.detail: He presented himself as a Hellenistic ruler of the West, married Theoxena, a stepdaughter of Ptolemy I, and gave his daughter Lanassa to Pyrrhus, linking Syracuse to the Epirote who would later claim Sicily as her heir.

events.title: Latin colony at Carseoli and the Marsic war
events.summary: A colony was voted for Carseoli in the former Aequian land in 302, and 4,000 colonists were sent in 298; when the Marsi resisted, the dictator M. Valerius Maximus defeated them and took Milionia, Plestina and Fresilia.
events.detail: Carseoli and Alba Fucens (303) secured the route of the later Via Valeria across the Apennines. Carseoli was one of the twelve Latin colonies that refused troops in 209.

events.title: Rome restores the Cilnii at Arretium
events.summary: When the people of Arretium rose to expel the powerful Cilnii family, Rome intervened; the dictator M. Valerius Maximus fought the Etruscans after his master of horse was ambushed, though Livy reports another version in which the Cilnii were simply reconciled with the plebs without war.
events.detail: The episode is the clearest instance of Rome backing Etruscan aristocracies against their commons, a pattern repeated at Volsinii in 265. Maecenas, Augustus' minister, descended from the Cilnii on his mother's side.
events.debate: Livy's sources disagreed on whether there was a war at all; the dictator is sometimes identified with Valerius Corvus.

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Salus; Fabius Pictor's paintings
events.summary: C. Junius Bubulcus, who had vowed a temple to Salus as consul in 311 and contracted it as censor in 307, dedicated it as dictator in 302; its walls were painted by C. Fabius, who took the cognomen Pictor, the first Roman noble known as a painter.
events.detail: The paintings survived until the temple burned under Claudius. Pliny and Valerius Maximus treat Fabius' choice of art as unusual for a patrician. His grandson Q. Fabius Pictor wrote the first Roman history in Greek around 200.

events.title: First barbers arrive from Sicily
events.summary: Varro records that barbers first came to Italy from Sicily in 300, brought by P. Titinius Mena; before then Romans went unshaven, as the long-bearded statues of the early Republic showed.
events.detail: Pliny adds that Scipio Aemilianus was the first to shave every day. The notice is a small but telling marker of the Hellenisation of Roman habits in the age of the Samnite wars.

events.title: Statues of Pythagoras and Alcibiades in the Comitium
events.summary: During the Samnite wars Apollo of Delphi told the Romans to set up statues of the bravest and the wisest of the Greeks in a busy place; they chose Alcibiades and Pythagoras and placed them at the corners of the Comitium, where they stood until Sulla rebuilt the Senate house.
events.detail: Pliny wondered why Socrates and Themistocles were passed over. The choice reflects the strong influence of the Italiote world, where Pythagoras had taught, on 4th-century Rome, and the tradition linking King Numa to Pythagoras.

events.title: Demetrius Poliorcetes complains of Antiate pirates
events.summary: Strabo records that Alexander, and later Demetrius Poliorcetes, sent back to Rome captured pirates from Antium, Demetrius remarking that it was wrong for the masters of Italy to send out pirates and to honour the Dioscuri in their Forum while allowing raids on the gods' own homeland.
events.detail: The anecdote shows Rome already seen in the Hellenistic East as the power responsible for central Italy, and that Antium's seamen kept raiding despite the ban on its fleet in 338. Its date falls in Demetrius' years of power, roughly 306-288.

events.title: Agathocles seizes Corcyra
events.summary: Agathocles broke Cassander's siege of Corcyra, took the island for himself, and later gave it as dowry when his daughter Lanassa married Pyrrhus of Epirus; Lanassa then left Pyrrhus and offered herself and the island to Demetrius Poliorcetes.
events.detail: The episode shows Syracuse playing in the politics of Alexander's Successors and explains Pyrrhus' later claims on Sicily through his son by Lanassa, Alexander.

events.title: Transalpine Gauls raid Etruria and Roman territory
events.summary: A new wave of Transalpine Gauls was bought off by the Cisalpine Celts and joined the Etruscans in a raid on Roman territory; they returned home with booty, quarrelled over it and destroyed most of their own army.
events.detail: Polybius places this after the thirty-year peace of 331; Livy says the Etruscans offered to pay the Gauls to fight Rome but they refused to settle. The episode foreshadows the Gallic-Samnite-Etruscan coalition defeated at Sentinum in 295.

events.title: Treaty with the Picentes
events.summary: Envoys of the Picentes warned Rome that the Samnites were seeking their alliance and obtained a treaty of friendship.
events.detail: The Picentes revolted in 269 and were crushed in 268, part of them being deported to the Gulf of Salerno.

events.title: Battle near Volaterrae
events.summary: L. Cornelius Scipio Barbatus fought the Etruscans near Volaterrae until nightfall; the Etruscans withdrew from their camp by night, leaving Rome the field, and the consul ravaged Etruscan territory.
events.detail: Livy's notice conflicts with Scipio's elogium, which mentions only Samnite and Lucanian successes, one of the classic problems in reconciling Livy with documentary evidence.

battle.significance: Drawn battle claimed as a victory.

events.debate: Conflict with the Scipio elogium over the consul's province in 298.

events.title: Volumnius surprises the Samnite raiders on the Volturnus
events.summary: Samnite bands plundering the Falernian and Campanian plains were caught by L. Volumnius as they withdrew laden with booty; he killed many, freed 7,400 prisoners and captured the Samnite general Staius Minatius.
events.detail: The raid prompted the Senate to found citizen colonies at Minturnae and Sinuessa to guard the coastal plain.

battle.significance: Protected Campania; led to the colonies of 296.

events.title: Fabius vows a temple to Jupiter Victor at Sentinum
events.summary: In the crisis of Sentinum Q. Fabius Rullianus vowed a temple and the enemy's spoils to Jupiter Victor; the temple, probably on the Palatine, is attested later.
events.detail: Sentinum produced several vows: the Ogulnii set up the she-wolf, Fabius dedicated Jupiter Victor, and Decius' devotio fulfilled a vow of a different kind.

events.title: Agathocles in southern Italy
events.summary: Agathocles took Croton by a ruse, allied with the Iapygians and Peucetians, to whom he gave pirate ships, and campaigned against the Bruttii, capturing Hipponion and building a harbour there.
events.detail: His Italian campaigns brought Syracusan power into the region Rome would contest with Pyrrhus fifteen years later. The Bruttii recovered Hipponion after his withdrawal.

events.title: Battle near Luceria and the vow to Jupiter Stator
events.summary: The consul M. Atilius Regulus, his camp attacked and his army giving way near Luceria, vowed a temple to Jupiter Stator, 'the Stayer'; the line held and the Samnites were defeated, 7,800 prisoners being sent under the yoke.
events.detail: Livy admits that his sources disagreed on whether Atilius won or was refused a triumph. The temple was built near the Porta Mugonia on the Palatine slope, on the spot where Romulus had vowed one in the Sabine war.

battle.significance: Restored Roman control of northern Apulia.

events.title: Postumius Megellus takes Rusellae
events.summary: The consul L. Postumius Megellus stormed the Etruscan city of Rusellae, taking over 2,000 prisoners.
events.detail: Rusellae's walls of large polygonal and squared blocks survive near Grosseto. It became a Roman ally and later supplied timber and grain for Scipio's fleet in 205.

events.title: Forty-year truces with Volsinii, Perusia and Arretium
events.summary: Volsinii, Perusia and Arretium sued for peace and obtained forty-year truces, each paying 500,000 asses; Postumius Megellus triumphed although the Senate refused, defying even the tribunes.
events.detail: The fines, expressed in bronze, show the scale of Etruscan wealth that Rome could extract. Megellus' illegal triumph was cited in his later trial.

events.title: Carvilius' colossal Jupiter on the Capitol
events.summary: From the breastplates, greaves and helmets of the Samnites killed at Aquilonia and Cominium, the consul Sp. Carvilius had a colossal bronze Jupiter cast for the Capitol, so large that it could be seen from the temple of Jupiter Latiaris on the Alban Mount; from the filings he made a statue of himself to stand at its feet.
events.detail: Carvilius also paid 380,000 asses of booty into the treasury, gave his soldiers 102 asses each and built a temple to Fors Fortuna across the Tiber. The colossus was among the first monumental bronzes made at Rome.

events.title: Temple of Fors Fortuna across the Tiber
events.summary: Sp. Carvilius built a temple of Fors Fortuna from Samnite spoils near the older shrine attributed to Servius Tullius, on the right bank of the Tiber.
events.detail: The festival of Fors Fortuna on 24 June was a popular holiday of boating and drinking, especially for the lower classes and slaves.

events.title: Postumius Megellus fined for using soldiers on his estate
events.summary: In his third consulship L. Postumius Megellus used 2,000 soldiers to clear woodland on his own estate and arrogantly overrode his colleague; after his term he was prosecuted and heavily fined.
events.detail: Dionysius' fragments preserve the case. Megellus had already triumphed in 294 against the Senate's will; in 282 he led the embassy to Tarentum whose humiliation began the Pyrrhic war.

events.title: The Esquiline historical painting (Fabius and Fannius)
events.summary: A fragment of fresco from a tomb on the Esquiline, painted in the early 3rd century, shows registers of battle and parley scenes with figures labelled Q. Fabius and M. Fannius, probably commemorating a Samnite war episode; it is the oldest surviving Roman historical painting.
events.detail: Found in 1875, it is now in the Capitoline collections (Centrale Montemartini). The Q. Fabius has been identified with Fabius Rullianus. It illustrates the genre of 'triumphal painting' that Romans carried in processions and displayed in temples.
scholarship: F. Coarelli, 'Frammento di affresco dall'Esquilino', in Roma medio repubblicana (1973)
events.debate: Date (late 4th to mid 3rd century) and identification of the figures are uncertain.

events.title: Lex Maenia: patrician approval given before elections
events.summary: A lex Maenia, of uncertain early 3rd-century date, required the patrician senators to give their sanction (auctoritas patrum) to elections in advance, extending to electoral assemblies the rule that the lex Publilia of 339 had applied to legislation.
events.detail: Cicero says that M'. Curius as tribune had forced the patres to approve a plebeian consul in advance, 'a great thing before the lex Maenia'. With the lex Hortensia (287), the law reduced the patrician veto to a formality, completing the legal side of the Struggle of the Orders.

events.title: Creation of the tresviri capitales
events.summary: The Periochae note that 'tresviri capitales were then created for the first time': three junior officials who ran the prison, supervised executions, policed the city at night and judged petty cases involving slaves and the poor at the Maenian column.
events.detail: They were later elected in the tribal assembly and formed part of the vigintisexvirate, the junior magistracies before the quaestorship. The moneyers (tresviri monetales) may date from the same reform.

events.title: Census of 289: about 272,000
events.summary: The Periochae record a lustrum with about 272,000 citizens counted in the late 290s or 289, the first census after the Third Samnite War.
events.detail: From the 290s Livy's figures, preserved in the Periochae, are widely accepted as genuine records of adult male citizens: 262,321 (293), c. 272,000 (289), 287,222 (280), 271,224 (275), 292,234 (265).

events.title: Death of Agathocles
events.summary: Agathocles died in 289 aged about 72, possibly poisoned at the instigation of his grandson Archagathus; before dying he restored 'democracy' to the Syracusans, refusing to name a successor, and his Campanian mercenaries were dismissed, to seize Messana as the Mamertines.
events.detail: Diodorus tells that the poison rotted his gums and that he was placed on the pyre while still alive. Syracuse fell into anarchy and the tyrannies of Hicetas and Phintias, until Pyrrhus (278) and Hiero II (275-215).

events.title: Lex Aquilia on wrongful damage
events.summary: A plebiscite carried by the tribune Aquilius, which Byzantine tradition dates to the secession of 287, laid down liability for wrongfully killing another's slave or four-footed herd animal (the highest value it had in the past year), for an accessory creditor's fraud, and for burning, breaking or spoiling (urere, frangere, rumpere) any other property (the value in the next thirty days).
events.detail: The law replaced scattered provisions of the Twelve Tables with a general regime of compensation for damnum iniuria datum. Over the following centuries jurists such as Labeo, Celsus and Ulpian extended it far beyond its words to cover negligence, indirect causation and personal injury to free persons, and it became the foundation of the law of delict in the civil-law tradition, still discussed in modern legal education. Ulpian notes it 'derogated from all earlier laws on damage'. The archaic valuation rules reflect a society of slaves and livestock and a period without coinage.
scholarship: Lawson and Markesinis, Tortious Liability for Unintentional Harm in the Common Law and the Civil Law (1982)
events.debate: Date: Theophilus' 287 is widely accepted but some argue for the later 3rd century.

events.title: Thurii appeals to Rome; statue of the tribune Aelius
events.summary: Attacked repeatedly by the Lucanians under Sthenius Statilius, the Greek city of Thurii turned to Rome rather than Tarentum; the tribune C. Aelius carried a measure against the Lucanian leader, and the grateful Thurians honoured him with a statue and a golden crown in Rome.
events.detail: Pliny saw this as the first Roman statue set up by a foreign people. In 282 Fabricius relieved Thurii and received a statue too. Rome's acceptance of a Greek city's appeal broke the spirit, if not the letter, of its treaty with Tarentum, and led to the war with Pyrrhus.

events.title: Roman garrisons in Thurii, Locri, Croton and Rhegium
events.summary: After Fabricius relieved Thurii, several Greek cities of the south received Roman garrisons against the Lucanians and Bruttii: Thurii, Locri, Croton and Rhegium, the last held by a legion of 4,000 Campanians under Decius Vibellius.
events.detail: The garrisons alarmed Tarentum and were the background to the attack on the Roman squadron. Locri soon expelled its Romans in favour of Pyrrhus, and the Campanian legion seized Rhegium for itself (280).

events.title: Phintias of Acragas moves Gela to a new city
events.summary: Phintias, tyrant of Acragas, destroyed Gela and moved its population to a new city he named after himself at the mouth of the Himeras, modern Licata.
events.detail: Phintias' rivalry with Hicetas of Syracuse, both defeated by Carthage, typifies the chaos in Sicily after Agathocles that opened the door to Pyrrhus and then to Rome and Carthage.

events.title: Aemilius Barbula ravages the Tarentine territory
events.summary: The consul L. Aemilius Barbula, sent from Samnium against Tarentum, defeated a Tarentine army and ravaged the land while offering peace; when Pyrrhus' advance guard under Milo arrived, he withdrew along the coast, shielding his column from attacks by ships with Tarentine prisoners placed on the seaward side.
events.detail: Barbula's triumph of 280 over the Tarentines, Samnites and Sallentines is in the Fasti. His campaign shows that Rome tried a short punitive war before Pyrrhus turned it into a major one.

battle.significance: Opening campaign of the Pyrrhic war.

events.title: Coruncanius triumphs over Volsinii and Vulci
events.summary: While Pyrrhus invaded the south, the consul Ti. Coruncanius defeated the Etruscan cities of Volsinii and Vulci, triumphing in 280; Vulci lost its coastal territory, where the Latin colony of Cosa was founded in 273.
events.detail: Coruncanius, from Tusculum, was the first plebeian pontifex maximus (c. 254) and the first to give public instruction in law. His Etruscan victory prevented a northern front during the Pyrrhic war.

events.title: Census of 280 and the first plebeian lustrum
events.summary: The censors of 280 counted 287,222 citizens, and Cn. Domitius Calvinus Maximus became the first plebeian censor to perform the lustrum, the purificatory sacrifice that closed the census.
events.detail: Plebeians had been eligible for the censorship since 351 and one censor had to be plebeian from 339, but the ritual act of the lustrum had remained in patrician hands. Domitius, consul in 283 and dictator in 280, was the founder of the Domitian line that later produced the emperor Nero.

events.title: Fabricius' embassy to Pyrrhus
events.summary: After Heraclea, C. Fabricius went to Pyrrhus to negotiate the return of prisoners; the king offered him gold and, the next day, tried to frighten him with an elephant trumpeting behind a curtain, but Fabricius was unmoved by either, and Pyrrhus let the prisoners go home on parole for the Saturnalia.
events.detail: Plutarch adds a conversation in which Cineas explained Epicurean philosophy and Fabricius wished such doctrines on Rome's enemies. The prisoners all returned as promised when the Senate refused peace. These stories built Fabricius into the archetype of incorruptible Roman poverty.

events.title: The Gauls invade Greece and attack Delphi
events.summary: A great Celtic migration killed Ptolemy Keraunos of Macedon in 279; one army under a Brennus forced Thermopylae and attacked Delphi, where it was repulsed by the Aetolians and Phocians in snow and earthquakes, and Brennus killed himself; other bands crossed to Asia in 278 to become the Galatians.
events.detail: Greeks celebrated the deliverance with the Soteria festival at Delphi. The invasion is part of the same Celtic movement that brought new bands into Italy in 299 and 284. In Rome's tradition a Brennus also led the Gauls of 390, an identity of name that may reflect a title or later borrowing.

events.title: The privileged treaty with Heraclea
events.summary: In 278 Heraclea in Lucania broke with Pyrrhus and concluded a treaty with Rome, negotiated by Fabricius, that Cicero called 'almost unique' in its favourable terms; the city valued it so highly that in 89 it hesitated to exchange it for Roman citizenship.
events.detail: Cicero's speeches for Balbus and Archias (the poet Archias was a citizen of Heraclea) are the source. The treaty illustrates how Rome detached Pyrrhus' Greek allies with generous terms.

events.title: Temple of Summanus
events.summary: When the terracotta Summanus on the roof of the Capitoline temple was struck by lightning and its head was lost, the haruspices found it in the Tiber; a temple of Summanus, god of nocturnal thunder, was dedicated by the Circus Maximus on 20 June, 'when Pyrrhus was feared'.
events.detail: Summanus was a little-understood god already by Ovid's time. The episode shows the role of Etruscan haruspices in interpreting lightning, their speciality.

events.title: Roman defeat in the Cranita hills
events.summary: With Pyrrhus in Sicily, the consuls P. Cornelius Rufinus and C. Junius Bubulcus invaded Samnium; the Samnites withdrew to the wooded Cranita hills, and a Roman assault up through the thickets was beaten back with heavy losses, after which the consuls quarrelled and divided their armies.
events.detail: Zonaras, abbreviating Dio, is the only source. The Samnites remained in arms until 272.

battle.significance: Showed continued Samnite resilience in the Pyrrhic war.

events.title: Rufinus takes Croton by a ruse
events.summary: P. Cornelius Rufinus sent a false deserter to Croton to report that he was withdrawing; Pyrrhus' general Nicomachus left with his garrison for Locri, and Rufinus seized the city; Locri then massacred its Epirote garrison and returned to Rome.
events.detail: The ruse is in Frontinus' collection of stratagems. Rufinus was expelled from the Senate in 275 for owning ten pounds of silver plate.

battle.significance: Deprived Pyrrhus of key Italiote allies.

events.title: Pyrrhus plunders the treasure of Persephone at Locri
events.summary: Returning from Sicily short of money, Pyrrhus punished Locri for going over to Rome and took the sacred treasure of Persephone's temple; the ships carrying it were wrecked and the treasure washed ashore, and Pyrrhus restored it in fear of the goddess.
events.detail: The story was told by the Locrians themselves in 204, when they complained to the Senate that Scipio's legate Pleminius had robbed the same temple, and Livy, Dionysius and Appian preserve it. Ancient writers saw Pyrrhus' later defeats as divine punishment.

events.title: Plague among women and cattle
events.summary: A pestilence struck pregnant women and livestock, causing stillbirths and the deaths of mothers and calves, so that Orosius says the Romans feared their stock would fail.
events.detail: The plague followed the introduction of Aesculapius (291) and coincided with the strains of the Pyrrhic war.

events.title: Hiero elected general at Syracuse
events.summary: After Pyrrhus left Sicily the Syracusan army, camped at Mergane, chose Hiero and Artemidorus as generals; Hiero entered the city, reconciled the factions, married the daughter of the leading citizen Leptines, and rid himself of his unruly mercenaries by sending them against the Mamertines without support.
events.detail: Polybius' account is admiring: Hiero became king after the victory at the Longanus (269) and ruled to 215 as Rome's most faithful ally from 263, the period of Archimedes, the Lex Hieronica grain tithe, and the great altar of Syracuse.

events.title: Curius' triumph and the first elephants in Rome
events.summary: M'. Curius Dentatus triumphed over the Samnites and Pyrrhus with a procession that showed Rome for the first time gold, purple, Greek statues and paintings, and four captured elephants with their towers.
events.detail: Pliny says Romans had first seen elephants at Heraclea in 280 and called them 'Lucanian oxen', and that they first appeared at Rome in this triumph. Florus contrasts it with earlier triumphs, which had displayed only cattle and Sabine wagons. Curius used his booty to build the Anio Vetus aqueduct (272).

events.title: Curius sells a draft-dodger
events.summary: When a citizen failed to answer the levy against Pyrrhus, the consul Curius had his property sold, and when he appealed to the tribunes, sold the man himself, saying that the state had no need of a citizen who would not obey.
events.detail: This is the earliest recorded case of a defaulter (infrequens) being sold into slavery, a penalty later used in exceptional crises. The story belongs to the exemplary tradition of Curius' severity and frugality.

events.title: Locri's coin of Roma crowned by Faith
events.summary: A silver stater of Locri shows a seated goddess labelled ROMA being crowned by a standing figure labelled PISTIS (Good Faith), with a head of Zeus on the obverse: the earliest known image of personified Roma, struck when Locri returned to the Roman alliance after Pyrrhus.
events.detail: The coin, usually dated c. 275-270, translates the Roman concept of fides into Greek visual language and anticipates the cult of Roma that Greek cities would establish in the 2nd century (Smyrna 195). It is a sought-after piece in the Magna Graecia series.
scholarship: R. Mellor, ThEA ROMH: The Worship of the Goddess Roma in the Greek World (1975)

events.title: Aes signatum: the elephant and sow bar
events.summary: Among the cast bronze bars of about five Roman pounds (c. 1.6 kg) issued by Rome in the 3rd century, one type shows an elephant on one side and a sow on the other, generally linked to the Pyrrhic war; other types show an eagle and Pegasus with the legend ROMANOM.
events.detail: Crawford dated the currency bars to c. 280-242, alongside the earliest cast aes grave. The sow may allude to the story that the Romans routed Pyrrhus' elephants with squealing pigs, or simply to sacrifice. Pliny's belief that early bronze was 'marked with cattle' (nota pecudum), from which pecunia derived, may reflect such bars.
events.debate: Dating and the meaning of the sow are disputed.

events.title: Vestals Sextilia and Caparronia condemned
events.summary: During the Pyrrhic war the Vestal Sextilia was convicted of unchastity and buried alive; in 266 the Vestal Caparronia hanged herself before trial, and her lover and the slave who abetted them were executed.
events.detail: The cases are recorded in the Periochae and Orosius from Livy's lost books. They fit the pattern of Vestal trials in periods of military strain.

events.title: Temple of Consus on the Aventine
events.summary: L. Papirius Cursor, victor at Tarentum in 272, dedicated a temple to Consus on the Aventine and had himself painted in it wearing triumphal dress.
events.detail: Festus records the painting along with that of M. Fulvius Flaccus in the temple of Vortumnus. Consus, the god of stored grain, also had an underground altar in the Circus Maximus.

events.title: Temple of Tellus vowed during the earthquake
events.summary: When the earth shook during the battle against the Picentes, the consul P. Sempronius Sophus vowed a temple to Tellus, Mother Earth; it was built on the Carinae on the site of the house of Sp. Cassius, razed in 485.
events.detail: The temple became a meeting place of the Senate (Antony convened it there after Caesar's murder) and held a map of Italy painted on its wall, described by Varro.

events.title: Temple of Pales vowed in the Sallentine war
events.summary: In the war against the Sallentini, which brought Brundisium into Rome's hands, the consul M. Atilius Regulus vowed a temple to Pales, the shepherds' deity whose festival, the Parilia of 21 April, was the birthday of Rome.
events.detail: Florus says that 'Pales herself demanded a temple' as the price of victory. The site of the temple is unknown.

events.title: Temple of Vortumnus from the spoils of Volsinii
events.summary: M. Fulvius Flaccus, who destroyed Volsinii, brought its god Vortumnus to Rome, probably by evocatio, dedicated a temple to him on the Aventine and had himself painted inside in triumphal dress; Pliny says 2,000 statues were taken from the city.
events.detail: Propertius makes Vertumnus a god of Etruscan origin standing in the Vicus Tuscus. The capture of Volsinii, seat of the Etruscan federal sanctuary, symbolically ended Etruscan independence; the bases of the dedications found at Sant'Omobono may come from its spoils.
